abstract: My background in scholarly publishing and peer review brought me to the United States to teach Scholarly Communication at the School of Information Sciences of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). Offering a course dedicated to the scholarly communication process is a fairly new endeavour for iSchools. In 2022, I was entrusted with a Scholarly Communication course composed of masters students in the Library & Information Science and the PhD in Information Sciences programs. The Scholarly Communication course was created by Prof. Dr. Maria Bonn, who is one of the authors of The Scholarly Communication Notebook (https://oercommons.org/hubs/SCN), ‘an active, inclusive, empowered community of practice for teaching scholarly communication to emerging librarians’. As Professor Bonn used to do with her library science students at the University of Illinois (Bonn 2014), in one of the first class sessions the students and I spent some time browsing job advertisements for Scholarly Communication librarians published on the ALA Job List (https://joblist.ala.org/). In these job advertisements posted from 2006 to 2014, we found positions titled ‘Scholarly Communications Librarian’, or others with a more specific focus such as ‘Copyright Librarian’, ‘Data Librarian’, or ‘Open Access and Intellectual Property Librarian’, and analysed the prevalence of scholarly communications terms, concepts, and activities, as identified by Finlay et al. (2015, 21), namely ‘instruction; digital products; outreach and liaison work; publishing; repositories; copyright, policy, and licensing; preservation; metadata, standards, and data management; and open access’. My students and I were particularly intrigued by the absence of peer review as one of the concepts requested of a scholarly communication position, since peer review is clearly represented in the schematic of the scholarly communication cycle created by the Association of College and Research Libraries (Figure 1, ACRL). Furthermore, the definition of scholarly communication librarianship of the ACRL includes the evaluation of scholarly work in peer-reviewed. journals: ‘the system through which research and other scholarly writings are created, evaluated for quality, disseminated to the scholarly community, and preserved for future use. The system includes both formal means of communication, such as publication in peer-reviewed journals, and informal channels, such as electronic listservs’ (ACRL 2003). In addition, as Meadows (1998, preface) says ‘Communication lies at the heart of research. It is as vital for research as the actual investigation itself, for research cannot properly claim that name until it has been scrutinized and accepted by colleagues’. This statement highlights that peer review is a fundamental aspect of the communication of research in scholarly publishing. Thus, I asked my students: Why is peer review not listed as a required competency for Scholarly Communication Librarians? Do you think that one day we will have a Peer Review Librarian? What can librarians do to support education in peer review? Motivated by these ideas, I (a peer review researcher with a PhD in Information Sciences, but no library science degree) designed and delivered an in-person and online peer review workshop curriculum for the Savvy Researcher workshop series sponsored by the University Library and supported by the School of Information Sciences at UIUC. The Savvy Researcher focuses on a variety of topics related to the lifecycle of research including advanced research and information management topics, for example, introduction to library resources, using tools to perform qualitative and quantitative research, data management, understanding copyright, and much more. All campus affiliates are invited to participate in the synchronous in-person and online sessions, including undergraduate and graduate students, campus staff, researchers, and faculty. Many of the workshops are concept-based around an assortment of scholarly communication topics, while others focus on a particular tool or library resource. The workshops are taught by librarians, graduate students in information science, and several campus partners such as the Center for Innovation in Teaching and Learning, the Writers Workshop, and the UI Press. In this article, I introduce the six-part peer review series ‘Peer Review in Scholarly Journals: History, People, and Models’ delivered at UIUC, and the lessons learned from the experience of conducting them. Finally, my coauthors and I offer recommendations on how peer review training could be improved and discuss the fundamental role of librarians in supporting peer review training. The six-part peer review series ‘Peer Review in Scholarly Journals: History, People, and Models’ was presented as a pilot offering during the fall semester and took place at the University Library from October 11, 2023 to November 15, 2023 (Figure 2). These new workshops were included on the Library's calendar and advertised broadly across campus throughout the fall semester. According to research programs liaison and instruction librarian and associate professor Merinda Kaye Hensley, who supported this initiative, the Peer Review Workshop Series was the first of its kind offered by the University Library. The purpose of the series was to educate a diverse audience and raise awareness regarding the goals and challenges of the peer review process implemented by scholarly journals, including current models and the role of reviewers. Since the sessions were not designed around any specific discipline, myriad examples of peer review were highlighted. The workshops were held for a duration of 60–90 min. Please see the Appendix A for details regarding the content of the workshops. Despite our efforts to promote the peer review workshops and be inclusive by opening registration to any member of the UIUC community, the first set of workshops had low attendance (Figure 3A). In the past 15 years, this is not an unusual occurrence for newly added workshops. Of the 26 total registrations across 6 scheduled sessions, only 10 registrants attended the workshops (Figure 3B). All attendees were graduate students with little to no experience with publishing and/or reviewing papers. The single exception was an editor that reached out directly by email to schedule a one-on-one appointment via Zoom to discuss the last workshop of the series, ‘Understanding and Implementing Open Peer Review.’ However, even with low attendance, offering workshops and sharing their descriptions across campus is a powerful tool to better inform campus stakeholders about the wide variety of topics, including complex scholarly communication issues, where librarians can help them with sharing, presenting, and archiving their scholarly work. We expected to see increased attendance at future workshops, as word-of-mouth spread. We also conducted a second set of non-consecutive sessions in Spring and Fall 2024. These were training sessions for undergraduate students working for an undergraduate research journal. As there was limited interest in the open peer review session previously, this was not conducted. Thus, in the undergraduate sessions, we had a total of 46 attendees split between five sessions (Figure 4). These sessions were better attended compared to the open Savvy Workshop ones. Even for an audience actively engaged as editorial staff and peer reviewers in a journal, interest waned as the specificity of themes progressed, and attendance at the last session was reduced to a third of the attendance of the introductory one. To evaluate the workshops, an auto generated form was sent to all registrants two days after each workshop. The workshop, ‘Reviewers and Their Biases’ was the only session that received feedback from an attendee. In the form, when asked ‘Did the workshop cover the content you expected?’ the attendee replied, ‘Sort of. The workshop helped show how to identify bias, but I was looking for techniques to address bias as well. For example, specific actions or ways I can avoid it when I review papers. Overall the workshop provided a good overview of what bias is and common types of biases during the peer-review process.’ When asked about their preference for the format of workshops, this attendee answered ‘in-person’. Additionally, one faculty member sent an email to the workshop instructor stating that one of their students attended a workshop and as a faculty member they would recommend it to their students. After this first experience in offering a peer review workshop series in an academic library, my coauthors and I reflected on how we could improve this initiative to better serve our campus stakeholders. Our improvement strategies for the pilot series are based on the identification of issues and questions that arose and how they could be addressed, namely by updating workshop content according to information needs of researchers at different career stages, providing additional opportunities for hands-on experience, offering workshops online and asynchronously, inviting scholarly communications stakeholders to speak of their perspective on the peer review process, identifying avenues to engage with undergraduate researchers, and possibly rethinking workshop titles to be more descriptive and actionable. During the workshop series, the workshop instructor observed that it is fundamental to reintroduce attendees to the foundational concepts of the peer review process for each workshop. This introduction contained definitions of the peer review process, the roles of editors, peer reviewers, and authors in relation to the manuscript, and introduction to peer review models, from traditional to open. This was imperative because workshop attendees were different each week, self-selected into the sessions, and the group did not share a common level of knowledge and understanding of the peer review process. Moreover, when showing examples of peer review policies and reviewer guidelines, it was noted that concepts such as originality, validity, and reproducibility were not clear to graduate students, a similar observation as that of Chong (2021, 464). Klebel et al. (2020) found that 75% of the top 100 journals (as per their 5-year h-index metric) surveyed had no clear policy with respect to whether co-reviewing was allowed, whether preprints could be cited, or if reviewer identities were published. This was true in subjects spanning Art, Economics, and Medical Sciences. Additionally, 30% of these journals did not offer clear information on which type of peer review was employed. However, this study was published in 2020 (Klebel et al. 2020), and the prevailing situation may have changed in recent years. After the torrent of retractions in 2023 and fears pertaining to paper mills and the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI), publishers have revised policies and instructions for authors to include ever more detailed declarations, in an effort to promote clarity and guidance. Of the 20 openly available online peer review training identified by Willis et al. (2022), only one had early career researchers as a target audience. Academics engaged with research in teaching of peer review have pointed out that scholarly publishing and peer review are components neglected in undergraduate science education (Otto et al. 2023). Although the instructor's intention was to bring researchers at different career stages for a peer review training and conversation at the library, the workshop design may inadvertently have ignored issues of power imbalance in peer review. In a study of the implementation of peer review curriculum in undergraduate education, one student described considering it safer and more comfortable to share her thoughts on paper with other undergraduate students than in journal clubs with graduate students (Otto et al. 2023). This way, future peer review workshops need to take into consideration not only the overall gaps in peer review education to better meet the information needs of researchers at different stages of their career, but also the competitive, hierarchical, and sometimes oppressive academic environment. Furthermore, we observed that some attendees signed up for a peer review workshop, but asked questions spanning other aspects of scholarly publishing. Some attendees had never heard of open access, others asked about strategies to identify predatory journals, and still others asked where to find a ‘good’ journal to submit a paper. A study conducted by Hurrell et al. (2024) has shown that, in fact, graduate students are interested in learning about scholarly communication topics such as publishing timeline, peer review, journal quality/prestige, appropriate and ethical use of generative AI tools in research and writing, predatory publishers, publishing costs, writing, and disciplinary norms. Taking this into account, the peer review workshops may also provide an invaluable opportunity to advertise other services offered by the Library, and provide insights leading to the creation of other workshops with a focus on the scholarly communication cycle. Some attendees came to the workshop series with the expectation of reviewing a paper. This experience was not offered to them. However, they were provided with an activity to review the peer review reports published by journals guided by the outline for writing a review report created by PLOS (https://plos.org/resource/how-to-write-a-peer-review/). This activity was conceived to explore the educational potential of peer review reports, to encourage discussions about what a good review looks like and the role of an effective reviewer, and to share with attendees typical queries authors receive to improve their manuscripts. During the open discussion portion of the workshop, attendees evaluated this activity positively and were surprised to find that journals have started to publish peer review reports. For the future peer review workshops, we would like to explore partnerships with initiatives such as PREreview—a community and open platform for preprint review—to provide hands-on experience in peer review of preprints. title: Machine Learning in Acoustics: A Review and Open-source Repository
abstract: Acoustic data provide scientific and engineering insights in fields ranging from bioacoustics and communications to ocean and earth sciences. In this review, we survey recent advances and the transformative potential of machine learning (ML) in acoustics including deep learning (DL). Using the Python high-level programming language, we demonstrate a broad collection of ML techniques to detect and find patterns for classification, regression, and generation in acoustics data automatically. We have ML examples including acoustic data classification, generative modeling for spatial audio, and physics-informed neural networks. This work includes AcousticsML , a set of practical Jupyter notebook examples on GitHub demonstrating ML benefits and encouraging researchers and practitioners to apply reproducible data-driven approaches to acoustic challenges.

title: Mapping end-of-life care in India: a scoping review to identify gaps in policy, practice, and psychosocial support
abstract: BACKGROUND: Little about access to palliative and end-of-life care in India is known. AIM: To map various facets of end-of-life care in India, from perceptions of stakeholders to capacity and quality of care, training, and education, and to identify the current gaps in end-of-life care delivery. DESIGN: A scoping literature review was conducted, with the protocol registered on the Open Science Framework, on November 29, 2023 ( https://osf.io/twc9j ). DATA SOURCES: Between January 1, 1990, and May 31, 2024, an electronic literature search was conducted using the MEDLINE, SCOPUS, CINAHL, EMBASE, and PSYCHINFO databases, as well as citations and grey literature. RESULTS: The availability and accessibility of end-of-life care are limited to a few geographical regions, primarily urban areas. While some states have community-based programs, most end-of-life care practices are concentrated in hospitals, especially intensive care units. Patients frequently lack access to essential medications, such as morphine, as well as appropriately trained medical professionals and adequate infrastructure. Financial difficulties, limited knowledge, social stigma toward the terminally ill and dying, and the psychological and physical burdens of care add to the challenges faced by stakeholders. CONCLUSION: The availability and accessibility of end-of-life care in India are fragmented. A comprehensive strategy that includes policy and legislative reforms, education, and expanded palliative services is crucial for improving the quality of end-of-life care across the country.

title: Mapping the Preprint Landscape: A Bibliometric Analysis of Global Research Dissemination (2015–2024)
abstract: Abstract Preprints have become an increasingly important component of scholarly communication, offering rapid dissemination of research prior to formal peer review. This study presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of peer-reviewed, Scopus-indexed articles published between 2015 and 2024 that examine preprints, preprint platforms, and their relationship to open science. Using Bibliometrix and VOSviewer, this study analyzes 4,826 articles to identify publication trends, prolific authors, influential journals, collaboration patterns, and thematic research clusters. Results reveal a steady increase in scholarly attention toward preprints, with strong linkages to topics such as open access, research transparency, and rapid knowledge sharing. Thematic mapping highlights core research hotspots in policy development, platform infrastructure, and disciplinary differences in adoption, alongside emerging themes such as preprints in health crises and their role in equitable knowledge dissemination. The analysis also uncovers gaps in cross-disciplinary collaboration and qualitative assessments of preprint impact. Future trends point toward broader policy alignment, enhanced interdisciplinary networks, and deeper integration with open science frameworks. To accelerate adoption, stakeholders in related fields can promote preprints by raising institutional awareness, providing training on platform use, and encouraging journal and funder policies that recognize preprint contributions.

title: Modelling maternal cardiovascular adaptation to pregnancy: a scoping review
abstract: BACKGROUND: The maternal cardiovascular system undergoes a profound transformation during pregnancy. Disordered cardiovascular adaptation is associated with pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction; however, these complications remain challenging to predict and manage. Computational modelling presents an opportunity to study the maternal circulation with unprecedented flexibility. We conducted a scoping review to assess the potential utility of computational models for studying maternal cardiovascular adaptation to pregnancy and providing insights into disease. We aimed to identify research gaps and barriers to translating this emerging field into clinical practice. METHODS: Medline, Embase, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from 01/01/2013 to 01/09/2025, for articles related to computational haemodynamic models of pregnancy. English-language studies describing models of the maternal circulation in human pregnancy were identified. Information on system modelled, study design, participant or clinical specimen details, and key findings were extracted from original research studies and presented in a narrative synthesis. RESULTS: Of 662 citations, 37 met inclusion criteria, comprising 28 original research studies, two conference abstracts, and seven reviews. Amongst the original research studies, 27 were basic experimental papers and one was a retrospective cohort study. Nine experimental articles incorporated data from pregnant participants or clinical specimens into personalised models, with sample sizes between one and 21. Four of these included participants or specimens affected by hypertensive disorders of pregnancy or fetal growth restriction. The retrospective cohort study employed haemodynamic modelling to investigate blood loss in 480 patients with abnormally invasive placentas. Modelling approaches described included those simulating the entire maternal circulation, maternal cardiac remodelling, maternal renal autoregulation, the maternal pelvic circulation in isolation, uterine vascular adaptation, spiral artery remodelling, and blood flows within the placental intervillous space. CONCLUSIONS: Computational modelling could represent a powerful tool to advance understanding of maternal cardiovascular adaptation to pregnancy and guide future approaches to risk stratification, diagnosis, and management of pregnancy complications. Realising this promise will require cardiovascular models to be parameterised with scalable metrics, validated in large pregnancy cohorts, developed alongside robust computational processing pipelines, and integrated into existing clinical workflows. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: The review protocol was registered prospectively with the Open Science Framework (osf.io/v3968).

title: On the Application of Artificial Intelligence and Cloud-Native Computing to Clinical Research Information Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: The pharmaceutical and biotechnology sector is an intricate and rapidly evolving industry encompassing the full lifecycle of drugs, medicines, and clinical devices. Its growth is driven by factors such as the aging population, the rise in chronic diseases, and the increasing focus on personalized medicine. Nevertheless, it also faces significant challenges due to rising costs, increased complexity, and regulatory hurdles. Through a systematic literature review (SLR) as a research method combined with a comprehensive market analysis, this paper explores how several leading early-adopter healthcare companies are increasing their investments in computer-based clinical research information systems (CRISs) to sustain productivity, particularly through the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud-native computing. As an extension of this research, a novel 360-degree reference blueprint is proposed for the domain analysis of medical features within AI-powered CRIS applications. This theoretical framework specifically targets clinical trial management systems (CRIS-CTMSs). Additionally, a detailed review is presented of the leading commercial solutions, assessing their portfolios and business maturity, while highlighting major open innovation collaborations with prominent pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies.

title: Open Access Publishing in Nutrition and Dietetics: State of the Art and Future Directions
abstract: Open science encompasses a set of practices designed to make the entire scientific research lifecycle and its outputs freely and openly accessible to all levels of society (David 2004; Suber 2012). This approach is widely recognised as a fundamental force for greater openness and collaboration within the scientific community (Fecher and Friesike 2014; Rentier 2019; Anagnostou et al. 2021; Maedche et al. 2024). Open Access (OA), data and methodology sharing and open peer review are core tenets of open science. They foster accountability and trust by allowing for independent verification and replication of studies. This transparency also promotes a more collaborative scientific environment, where researchers can build on each other's work more effectively and innovatively (Vicente-Saez and Martinez-Fuentes 2018). The removal of paywalls and subscription barriers, a key principle of OA, accelerates scientific progress by making research knowledge accessible to a broad audience, including researchers, educators, policymakers and the public. Open practices are especially critical for Nutrition and Dietetics (N&D) because the field is inherently linked to public health and individual well-being, making the accurate and timely dissemination of information essential. They ensure the latest evidence is readily accessible, verifiable, and usable by all stakeholders. Unrestricted access to peer-reviewed nutritional research directly enables health professionals—such as physicians, nutritional biologists and nutritionists/dietitians—to update their practices with the most current evidence, providing patients with accurate and timely nutritional information (Capocasa and Venier 2023). This ability to stay current is also a vital global health consideration, given that a poor diet remains a leading risk factor for mortality and morbidity worldwide (Chan et al. 2009; GBD 2017 Diet Collaborators 2019). Moreover, open science expedites the translation of research findings into clinical practice and public health policy (Spedding 2016), while also fostering innovation and strengthening collaborations with industry for the development of novel technologies and solutions (Friesike et al. 2015; Vicente-Saez et al. 2020). This facilitates the broader dissemination of scientific information into comprehensible content, supporting informed health decisions for the general public and ultimately promoting overall well-being. Recognising the paramount importance of open practices in N&D, we explored the evolving landscape of OA, drawing comparisons with trends observed in other health and life sciences disciplines. Our analysis of N&D publications indexed by Web of Science [see Capocasa et al. (2025) (data and Supporting Information file in Zenodo—link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.2599965)] reveals a consistent OA rise between 2000 and 2023 (Figure 1). The OA rate more than doubled, climbing from 31.4% in 2000–2003 to 62.9% in 2020–2023, with an average annual increase of 1.3%. Looking more closely at recent years (2020–2023), it is evident that OA rates for publications that are usually subjected to peer review—such as articles (63.9%) and reviews (60.8%)—are above or closer to the overall average OA rate of 62.9% (which refers to all N&D publications in the same period, including research articles, reviews, editorials, letters, book chapters and proceedings papers; see Capocasa et al. 2025). Conversely, editorials (59.8%) and letters (49.8%) remain below this average. These lower OA rates may be partly due to many subscription-based journals making this content freely available without an OA licence, which reduces the incentive for authors to pay for OA. In addition, universities and research institutions are increasingly prioritising the reimbursement of Article Processing Charges (APCs) for articles published in OA journals. They are more likely to support articles that demonstrate higher levels of scientific quality and prestige, such as research articles and reviews, criteria that are often associated with a greater number of citations (Björk and Solomon 2015). This disparity suggests the influence of funding mandates and institutional policies. Major funders, such as UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and organisations participating in Plan S, explicitly require an OA licence for peer-reviewed outputs supported by their grants (Coalition S 2025; UK Research and Innovation 2023). Similarly, a growing number of university OA policies prioritise the deposit of final, revised manuscripts in institutional repositories (Harvard Library 2010; Oxford Brookes University 2025), further contributing to the observed trends. Beyond these policy-driven shifts, the COVID-19 pandemic also significantly impacted OA adoption (Lee and Haupt 2021; Riccaboni and Verginer 2022; Malkawi et al. 2023). The urgent global need for rapid knowledge sharing prompted publishers to waive APCs and funders to mandate OA for all COVID-19-related research, resulting in a notable surge in OA publications across diverse disciplines (Arrizabalaga et al. 2020; Capocasa et al. 2022; Sayer et al. 2023). Following the general trend, the OA rate of N&D was higher (an increase of 23.8%) than that of non-COVID-19 papers. However, the impact on overall OA rates was limited (+0.9%) due to the relatively low prevalence of COVID-19-related publications within our field (see Capocasa et al. 2025). As these policies have gained traction and evolved, the landscape of OA publishing has also shifted, leading to a preferred route for achieving OA. The Gold OA model—in which publishers make papers immediately and freely available, funded by APCs—has become the dominant route in scientific publishing, driven primarily by its immediate accessibility and alignment with funder and institutional mandates (Wang et al. 2018; Torres-Salinas et al. 2019). Alongside these advantages, a significant concern is the rise of predatory journals, which exploit APCs to publish articles without rigorous peer review (Shen and Björk 2015; Beall 2017). The surge in the OA model's popularity among authors stems from two main factors. As previously noted, many funding agencies and institutions now mandate OA publication, with grants often covering APCs to encourage authors to choose Gold OA (Mering 2020; Robinson-Garcia et al. 2020). This is further incentivised by the rise of transformative agreements, which are contracts between institutions and publishers that reallocate subscription fees to cover APCs, simplifying the OA transition and making it more attractive and accessible by reducing costs for individual researchers (Borrego et al. 2021; Moskovkin et al. 2022). Secondly, immediate OA significantly boosts research article visibility and impact, making content more discoverable and readable by a wider audience (Young and Brandes 2020). This increased exposure can lead to higher citation rates, a crucial metric for researchers and institutions (Lewis 2018; but see Langham-Putrow et al. 2021). Our analysis confirms a strong preference for the Gold OA route within N&D. Between 2020 and 2023, the majority of OA papers (86.4%) were published under a Creative Commons licence in either fully OA or hybrid journals, a trend that consistently increased throughout these 4 years (Figure 2). Notably, even within this dominant Gold OA trend, articles and reviews continue to lead the way (see Capocasa et al. 2025). Significantly, the Gold route has largely surpassed Bronze OA, where papers are readable but lack explicit reuse rights. However, the widespread adoption of Creative Commons licences brings with it a critical, yet often overlooked, issue: the complexity of these licences (Guibault 2008). Authors' limited understanding of the distinctions between licences and their impact on reuse and commercial rights can create hesitation. This knowledge gap is particularly critical in nutrition research, where the line between academic output and commercial application is often blurred. Conversely, we observed a decline in the Green OA road, where authors self-archive a version of a published manuscript, such as a pre-print or post-print, in an online institutional or disciplinary repository, showing again a consistent negative trend year by year (Figure 2). This OA model faces several challenges contributing to this outcome. For instance, embargo periods imposed by publishers reduce the immediate accessibility of research, potentially diminishing its impact both within and beyond academia (Koley and Lala 2022). Moreover, the existence of multiple article versions (pre-prints, post-prints) can lead to confusion regarding the authoritative version. Furthermore, complex and varied archiving policies create administrative burdens, sometimes making Green OA less appealing than Gold OA. Despite these challenges, Green OA remains a powerful and equitable option. It is a cost-effective pathway to meet OA mandates, particularly for researchers in low- and middle-income countries or those with limited institutional funds to cover APCs. Leveraging institutional and subject repositories is not just a secondary option, but a vital strategy to ensure that cost is never a barrier to knowledge sharing. Furthermore, Green OA can lead to citation rates at least comparable to those of Gold OA (Zhang and Watson 2017; Young and Brandes 2020), and if more fully leveraged without infringing publisher policies, it could significantly boost OA rates in biomedical research (Destro Bisol et al. 2022). How does N&D compare with other medical and biological fields in terms of OA rates? And what insights can we gain to identify facilitators and overcome barriers? A look at various disciplines reveals significant variation in OA rates, ranging from 42.5% in Anatomy and Morphology to 81.5% in Medicine, General and Internal (Figure 3). With N&D's OA rate (62.9%) falling slightly below the overall average (63.8%), it suggests this field has considerable potential for improvement. However, it is important to recognise that nutrition research often operates with more limited financial resources compared to other medical domains (Weaver and Miller 2017). Therefore, the APCs required by many Gold OA journals may slow the pace at which the field embraces broader OA adoption. In addition to this field-specific obstacle, a cultural barrier shared with other disciplines plays an important role. For many researchers, especially those in senior positions, the most prestigious and impactful work is still published in traditional, subscription-based journals like The New England Journal of Medicine and Nature. This creates a well documented ‘attitude–behaviour gap’ where their support for OA fails to translate into publishing behaviour (Köster et al. 2021). Senior researchers are often reluctant to publish their own high-impact work in OA journals for fear of it not being taken as seriously by promotion and tenure committees, a concern directly tied to how career advancement policies evaluate scholarly output (Pontika et al. 2022). Medicine, General & Internal, Medicine Research & Experimental, Oncology, and Genetics & Heredity stand out as fields with notably high OA rates, all exceeding 70%. Funder mandates probably play a pivotal role in elevating the adoption of OA in medical research. For instance, the National Institutes of Health (NIH), as the world's largest biomedical research agency, requires articles on biomedical and health topics funded by it to be submitted to its PubMed Central digital archive and made publicly accessible within 12 months of publication (National Institutes of Health 2025). Similarly, the Wellcome Trust and Cancer Research UK, leading global charitable foundations dedicated to improving health, require that all original published research they support—which heavily includes biomedical, clinical and genetics research—be made freely available from Europe PubMed Central upon publication, typically under a Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) licence (Cancer Research UK 2022; Wellcome Trust 2025). While the influence of mandates on OA rates is well established, the exceptionally high OA rate observed in Genetics points to another powerful underlying force: its inherent research culture. This field frequently generates and analyses massive datasets, often millions or even billions of data points per individual. Openly sharing these vast datasets is a fundamental prerequisite for large-scale, publicly funded initiatives, and this practice is inextricably linked to publishing research OA. This is because these open research outputs significantly accelerate scientific discovery and foster international collaboration, both of which are essential for the advancement of genetics research. The Human Genome Project (HGP), completed in 2003, serves as a paradigmatic example. It allowed researchers worldwide to access, analyse, and build upon the data without delay, leading to a much faster pace of discovery than would have been possible under a more restrictive, proprietary model. Another important aspect that may help achieve higher OA rates is the availability of reputable OA. Currently, the fields of Medicine, General and Internal and Oncology have significantly more OA journals indexed by Web of Science compared to N&D; 47.7% (157 of 329) of Medicine, General and Internal journals and 34.3% (109 of 318) of Oncology journals are OA, while only 20.4% (31 of 109) of N&D journals are. This disparity suggests that the limited number of OA publication venues in N&D might be hindering its OA growth. The data presented effectively underscores the dynamic evolution of OA within N&D. The consistent rise in OA adoption through time mirrors the broader global shift towards open science, signalling positive progress for the field. However, our analysis also reveals that OA rate, despite its growth, still lags slightly behind leading medical fields. This gap presents a clear opportunity for improvement. To bridge this divide and further accelerate OA in N&D, the field can draw valuable lessons from the successful strategies observed in biomedicine. These include the implementation of stronger funder requirements, the provision of robust institutional support for OA costs, and the widespread adoption of the Gold OA model, often facilitated by transformative agreements, along with fostering the growth of reputable N&D-specific OA journals, mirroring trends in fields like Medicine, General and Internal, and Oncology (Severin et al. 2020; Borrego et al. 2021). Furthermore, while Gold OA has become the preferred route, often empowered by the diffusion of transformative agreements, it is crucial not to overlook Green OA. Actively encouraging Green OA for researchers facing financial constraints, along with optimising repositories for immediate, non-embargoed versions of articles, would significantly enhance accessibility and ensure that cost is not a barrier to open knowledge sharing. By embracing these multi-faceted approaches, N&D can fully leverage the benefits of OA, fostering greater research visibility, collaboration, and ultimately, scientific advancement. Beyond these specific strategies, a supportive research culture is essential for continuously advancing open science within the dynamic landscape of scholarly communication. This necessitates collaborative action among researchers, institutions, funders and publishers. Community-driven strategies, as advocated by Tennant et al. (2016), are crucial for fostering transparency and cooperation. To achieve this, in N&D and elsewhere, it is vital to integrate Open Science values and skills into academic training, starting with early-career researchers and PhD students. Educating the next generation of scientists on topics like open data sharing, open peer review, and the use of repositories is a key step in embedding these practices into the scientific process (Destro Bisol et al. 2014; Schönbrodt 2019). Furthermore, coordinated interdisciplinary efforts, bringing together nutritionists, clinicians, and data experts, can innovate to broaden research reach and impact. The Open Science Collaboration (Nosek et al. 2015), with its model for cross-disciplinary partnerships and guidelines for transparency, openness, and reproducibility, exemplifies how research culture drives open practices. This interdisciplinary approach in nutrition not only enriches scientific discourse but also highlights OA's vital role in fostering collaborations and improving public health outcomes (Capocasa and Venier 2023, 2024). In summary, N&D's journey towards open science reflects a promising commitment, yet the field has a clear path to further solidify its OA standing. By strategically adopting established best practices from leading biomedical disciplines, particularly regarding funder mandates and institutional support, N&D can boost its OA rates. Crucially, fostering a robust research culture that champions transparency and collaboration across disciplines, while also leveraging both Gold and Green OA pathways, will be key. While expanded access to scientific knowledge is vital for providing precise information, it also brings inherent risks. When research is made openly accessible to the broader public, including media professionals, journalists and policymakers, there is a risk of misinterpreting complex, subtle, or early-stage results. This challenge arises because even OA scholarly articles often contain specialised and technical terminology that is difficult for a general audience to understand. Moreover, the scientific community continues to face difficulties in conveying research findings clearly and impactfully to non-specialists. Such communication barriers can contribute to the spread of false information, as evidenced by the prevalence of fake news concerning nutrition online (Capocasa and Venier 2023). Addressing these challenges requires parallel efforts in effective science communication and media literacy initiatives, ensuring that OA translates into accurate understanding and informed decision-making. By combining robust OA practices with targeted communication strategies, N&D can maximise the benefits of open science—enhancing knowledge accessibility, driving scientific discovery, and contributing more broadly to global health improvements—while mitigating the risks of public misunderstanding.
