title: The Use of Continuous Temperature Data from Wearable Devices for Fever or Infection Management in Acute Hospital Settings: A Scoping Review Protocol
abstract: Introduction Despite the increasing interest in wearable devices for monitoring body temperature in acute hospital settings, their integration into routine clinical workflows remains limited. There is a growing need to map the existing evidence on the use of temperature data generated by wearable devices to enhance our understanding of how these data are monitored, presented, and utilised in clinical practice. Methods and analysis A scoping review of relevant literature from January 2013 to February 2025 will be conducted following the Joanna Briggs Institute scoping review methodology. A search of Medline, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL, and IEEE Xplore Databases will be undertaken using the PCC (Population, Concept, Context) framework to identify studies that use wearable devices to monitor patients' body temperature in acute hospital settings to support the management of fever or infections. A pilot search has been conducted to identify key search terms and specific types of wearable devices followed by analysis of retrieved literature. We will use a two-step screening process to identify eligible articles, starting with title/abstract screening, followed by full-text screening. A hand search of the reference lists and citation lists of eligible articles and identified reviews will be conducted for additional publications that meet the inclusion criteria. Primary studies published in English and Chinese will be included regardless of their design and type of publication. Information on the characteristics of wearable devices, clinical contexts of device usage, strategies of presenting and analysing temperature data, and their integration into clinical workflows will be extracted. In the article presenting the results of the scoping review, we will provide a descriptive synthesis of the findings, supported by visual representations such as charts, tables, and images to describe the current evidence base. Ethics and dissemination As this is a scoping review, ethical approval is not required. The results will be presented in a peer-reviewed journal article and at healthcare or medical informatics conferences. The findings will provide insights into the interpretation of temperature data generated by wearable devices to support clinical decision-making and inform strategies to facilitate their incorporation into clinical practice. Registration This scoping review protocol is registered on Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/v6sp8).

title: Transferring Tech Recruiting Heuristics to Creative Engineering Domains: A Hybrid Skill Taxonomy Model for Sourcing Top-Tier Designers and Developers
source: International Journal of Applied Research in Business and Management
abstract: Few candidates will ever squeeze their elite designers and developers into conventional recruitment funnels; non-technical recruiters are especially found wanting in sourcing for creative engineering specialities. Herein, we present a hybrid skills framework enhanced by AI tools that enable recruiters to make confident hiring decisions without requiring in-depth domain knowledge. By merging algorithmic evaluation of candidate work products from GitHub, Figma, and Behance with natural language processing of voice-interview transcripts, our approach converts a subjective experience into a reproducible process driven by objective metrics. At its core lies the SNRHiring Index, a proprietary composite score computed from hard skills and behavioural stimuli verified against real-world digital signals. Built with scalability and transparency in mind, this framework has since been applied in a production setting for tech recruitment, reducing hiring time, increasing the quality-to-fit rate of portfolios, and improving post-hire retention. The conclusions, therefore, enable the building of a repeatable playbook for HR practitioners, startup CTOs, and HRTech researchers interested in innovating creative technical hiring. By affording clients the ability to source high-quality talent even without insider knowledge, this paper thus contributes not only to the AI-hiring literature but also to establishing a DOI-citable proof of method for platform credibility, investor assurance, and transparency to clients.

title: Un/Sustainable Peer Review and Generative AI: Ethical Gaps, Editorial Acceleration, and the Whitewashing of Technological Solutionism
source: Imaginations Journal of Cross-Cultural Image Studies
abstract: Generative AI in peer review raises ethical and environmental concerns and risks deepening existing inequities in scholarly publishing. Celebrated gains in speed often mask declines in quality and accountability. Training and deploying large models impose environmental costs. In editorial workflows, AI can privilege technical fixes over structural reform, and evidence shows it reproduces human biases while being cast as neutral. We call for a renewed commitment to open-science principles anchored in human oversight, deep sustainability, and broader justice. The paper concludes by interrogating sustainability’s absence from green-economy debates and mapping the values likely to shape the future of peer review.

title: Uncovering Phenotypes in Sensorineural Hearing Loss: A Systematic Review of Unsupervised Machine Learning Approaches
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The majority of the 1.5 billion people living with hearing loss are affected by sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). Reliably categorizing these individuals into distinct subtypes remains a significant challenge, which is a critical step for developing tailored treatment approaches. Unsupervised machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence (AI), offers a promising solution to this issue. However, no study has yet compared the outcomes of different AI models in this context. The purpose of this review is to synthesize the existing literature on the application of unsupervised machine learning models to hearing health data for identifying subtypes of SNHL. DESIGN: A systematic search was performed of the following databases: MEDLINE, PsycINFO (Ovid version), EMBASE, CINAHL, IEEE, and Scopus as well as a search of grey literature using GitHub and Base, and manual search (Jan 1990-Mar 2024). Studies were included only if they reported on adult patients with SNHL and used an unsupervised machine-learning approach. Quality assessment was performed using the APPRAISE-AI tool. The heterogeneity of studies necessitated a narrative synthesis of the results. RESULTS: Seven studies were included in the analysis. Apart from one case-control study, all were cohort studies. Four different algorithms were used, with no study comparing the performance of more than one algorithm. Across these studies, only 2 distinct numbers of subtypes were identified: 4 and 11. However, the overall quality of the studies was deemed low, thus preventing definitive conclusions regarding model selection and the actual number of subtypes. CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review identifies key methodological practices that need to be improved before the potential of unsupervised machine learning models to subtype SNHL can be realized. Future research in this field should justify model selection, ensure reproducibility, use high-quality hearing data, and validate model findings.

title: University Faculty Research Competence: A Systematic Literature Review of Core Components, Distinctions, and Measures
abstract: Recent studies identified that faculty research productivity increased when they felt competent in conducting research. Faculty level of research competency varies due to academic training, context, country, discipline, and experiences; however, what is faculty research competency? The core competencies of faculty research are unclear; thus, the current study systematically reviewed the literature. Researchers used Boolean searches of four popular databases to identify 553 articles for first-level screening. These yielded 46 peer-reviewed journal articles for full-text analysis, six of which focused on faculty populations (40 on non-faculty). Six core components of faculty research proficiency were identified: finding and reviewing literature, planning a study, collecting and analyzing data, writing research, disseminating research findings, and managing research projects. Compared to non-faculty populations, faculty are uniquely more engaged in research project management. Researchers also identified 18 sub-competencies that will help to measure faculty research competency more reliably in the future. Finally, as the identified studies relied on self-reported measurements that may carry self-representation bias, an aspirational implication is to develop a competency-based diagnostic test for measuring faculty research competence.

title: Using expert knowledge and peer review to create a reproducible process for the NAHRS Nursing Essential Resources List (NNERL)
source: Journal of the Medical Library Association JMLA
abstract: Background: Librarians have relied on resource lists for developing nursing collections, but these lists are usually in static or subscription-based formats. An example of this is the 26th edition of the Essential Nursing Resources last published in 2012. The Nursing and Allied Health Resources and Services (NAHRS) Caucus Nursing Essential Resources List (NNERL) Task Force has been working on a new list since Fall 2020. The goal of the Task Force is to create a nursing resource list that represents current materials and formats, uses a selection process that is transparent and reproducible, and will be available to a broad audience. Case Presentation: Working from the Essential Nursing Resources 26th edition, the NNERL Task Force updated the purpose statement then began reviewing the resources on the list. Two working groups were formed: 1) an evaluation rubric working group developed a tool to evaluate the resources and 2) a tagging work group developed guidelines for creating metadata and "tags." Volunteers were recruited from the NAHRS Caucus to tag the resources. Lastly, the Task Force finalized the list of resources in the NNERL then cleaned and reconciled the data. Conclusions: The final version of the NNERL will be published in Airtable, a cloud-based project management product, that will include metadata for every item on the list. The NNERL will be copyrighted to the NAHRS NNERL Task Force and made available through the Open Science Framework (OSF) under an Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International Creative Commons License.

title: Utilization of Oxford Nanopore Technology for human infectious disease detection and surveillance in Africa: a scoping review
abstract: Background. Nanopore‐based sequencing by Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) offers rapid, cost‐effective and portable sequencing. As an emerging technology, ONT must be evaluated for efficacy and practical application in both high‐ and low‐resource settings. This scoping review (SR) aimed to (1) describe how nanopore technology is used in Africa for surveillance and diagnosis of human infectious diseases, (2) describe how nanopore technology aids in the real-time detection of infectious pathogens in Africa and (3) identify challenges and opportunities for utilizing nanopore technology in Africa to study infectious diseases. Methods. This SR followed the Joanna Briggs Institute Reviewer’s Manual framework for SRs. English language studies published from 1 January 2008 to 30 April 2024 that used ONT on human specimens collected in Africa and targeted ≥1 microbial agent were included. Searches were performed in Embase, Medline, PubMed, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library. The protocol was publicly available on the Open Science Framework Bastug et al. (Nanopore Sequencing for Infectious Diseases Surveillance and Diagnostics in Africa: a Scoping Review 2024) prior to data collection. Two independent reviewers screened studies using Covidence, and data was extracted using a custom REDCap instrument. Descriptive statistics and data visualization were performed in Microsoft Excel. Results. One thousand one hundred sixty-two studies were identified and 93 (8%) underwent full-text review. The portable MinION Mk1B was the most common ONT device (65% of studies). Eighty-eight studies analysed specimens from a single African country. Of these, 45% were sequenced in the same country, 7% in a different African country and 11% in a non-African country, while 32% did not specify the location. Specimen types included direct patient specimens (62%) and cultured isolates (35%), or a combination of both. Blood, serum or plasma was most common (35%), followed by naso- or oropharyngeal specimens (27%). Forty-four studies used ONT during an active infectious disease outbreak, 25 of which studied severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Seventy-two studies used ONT for genomic surveillance of infectious pathogens or antibiotic resistance genes, and one study used ONT for a direct clinical application. African-affiliated authors were included as first, middle and last authors in 46% of studies, and 15% were published by entirely African-affiliated teams. Ten studies published information on workflow timeline, and five studies published the per-specimen cost. Conclusions. ONT can enable timely and affordable sequencing in African countries as demonstrated through a small number of studies that accomplished these goals individually. Most studies used ONT for genomic surveillance of pathogens or antimicrobial resistance genes, while only one study used ONT directly for a real-time clinical application. A small number of studies described a short interval between specimen collection and sequence result, supporting that clinical applications are possible. There is a need for improved reporting of ONT methodology including pipeline timelines, cost, use of barcoding, flow cell models and the use of negative controls. Publications that provide these details will enhance reproducibility and support the development of new studies using ONT for the diagnosis and surveillance of infectious diseases in low-resource settings.

title: Waterfall Model Simulation: A Systematic Mapping Study
abstract: This paper systematically maps peer-reviewed research and graduate theses/dissertations that explicitly simulate the waterfall model. Following Petersen's mapping guidelines and Kitchenham's systematic literature review practices, major databases (ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Springer, Google Scholar, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between 2000-2024 using the title query ("simulation" OR "simulating") AND "waterfall". A PRISMA workflow guided the screening process, and approximately 9% of retrieved records met the inclusion criteria. A repeated extraction process captured methods, tools, venues, geography, publication years, comparative scope, and fidelity to Royce's original model; findings were synthesized thematically. Discrete-event simulation dominates (80%) compared to system dynamics (20%). Reported tools center on Simphony.NET (40%) and SimPy (20%), while 40% of studies omit tool details, limiting reproducibility. Research is distributed across Italy, Lebanon, India, Japan, and the United States; publication venues include 60% journals and 40% conferences. Sixty percent of studies are comparative, while 40% model only the waterfall approach. No study reproduces Royce's original model; all employ adaptations. The paper concludes by presenting a consolidated view of waterfall simulation research and recommending clearer model reporting, fuller tool disclosure, and wider adoption of open-source platforms.

title: Whole blood transfusion in the management of obstetric hemorrhage: A scoping review
abstract: Obstetric hemorrhage remains a major cause of maternal mortality worldwide.1 Standard management strategies include uterotonics, tranexamic acid (TXA), balloon tamponade, embolization, and surgical intervention.2 In cases of severe hemorrhage, transfusion support is typically provided using component-based therapy, which includes packed red blood cells (PRBCs), plasma, and platelet concentrates administered in empiric ratios.3, 4 While this approach is widely used, it presents logistical challenges related to product preparation (e.g., thawing plasma), transport coordination, and simultaneous bedside administration of multiple components. Additionally, there is uncertainty regarding optimal transfusion ratios, especially in urgent or resource-limited settings. Whole blood (WB) transfusion has re-emerged as an alternative strategy for managing hemorrhage in trauma and military contexts.5-7 Unlike component-based transfusions, WB contains red blood cells, plasma, and platelets in physiologic ratios, allowing for simplified and potentially more efficient resuscitation compared to component-based therapy.5-7 These properties suggest a possible role for WB in obstetric hemorrhage, where rapid and coordinated transfusion is critical. Despite its increasing use in trauma care, the application of WB transfusion in obstetric settings remains underexplored.8 Existing studies from trauma populations suggest potential benefits,5, 6, 9 but differences in physiology and mechanisms of bleeding between trauma and obstetric patients may limit generalizability. Furthermore, the use of RhD-positive WB in emergencies presents a risk of alloimmunization in RhD-negative females of childbearing potential, with implications for future pregnancies due to the risk of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN).10 This scoping review aims to describe the current literature on WB transfusion in obstetric hemorrhage, focusing on maternal outcomes, transfusion-related complications, and the comparative effectiveness of WB versus component-based approaches. We conducted this scoping review following the methodological guidance of the Joanna Briggs Institute.11 We prospectively registered the review protocol on the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/65B89). We reported the review in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines (Appendix A).12 Our research team included experts in transfusion medicine, obstetrics, anesthesiology, and critical care. We included studies that enrolled pregnant women with obstetric hemorrhage, evaluated WB transfusion, and reported maternal outcomes such as morbidity (e.g., transfusion-related complications, intensive care unit [ICU] admission, pulmonary edema, adult respiratory distress, acute kidney injury) or mortality. We considered peer-reviewed randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, case–control studies, and case series published in English or French. We excluded opinion pieces, editorials, letters, and non-peer-reviewed articles. We applied no restrictions on patient age or publication date. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, Scopus, Cochrane Library, ERIC, Web of Science, and CINAHL from inception to June 11, 2025. We developed the electronic search strategy (see Appendix B) in collaboration with an information specialist, and a second specialist peer-reviewed it according to PRESS guidelines.13 We also searched gray literature via Google Scholar and manually reviewed reference lists from the included studies. We used a three-stage screening process. Two pairs of reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts in Covidence (version 2.0, Veritas Health Innovation). They resolved disagreements through consensus or, if necessary, involved a third reviewer. Two authors independently reviewed the full-text articles that met inclusion criteria, resolving discrepancies by consensus. Two reviewers independently extracted data using standardized forms that captured study design, participant characteristics, interventions, and outcomes. They resolved any discrepancies through discussion and consensus. We measured outcomes including severe maternal morbidity (SMM), maternal mortality, and WB transfusion efficacy. Morbidity outcomes included postpartum hemorrhage requiring hysterectomy, uterine rupture, ICU admission, transfusion-related reactions, and thromboembolic events, as defined in prior large-scale studies.14 We also assessed mortality within 3–6 hours post-intervention based on recent recommendations.15 We evaluated transfusion efficacy by documenting the number of WB units administered and clinical responses such as reversal of hemorrhagic shock, vital sign stabilization, and the need for additional surgery. We did not perform a formal quality assessment, as scoping review methodology does not require it.16, 17 We did not seek ethics approval because we analyzed only publicly available literature and did not involve primary data collection or direct interaction with human participants. The initial search identified 2886 articles across selected electronic databases (Figure 1). After removing 1216 duplicates, 1670 unique records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 1636 were excluded, and 34 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Following full-text review, 26 articles were excluded, resulting in eight studies meeting inclusion criteria for this scoping review.18-25 The eight included studies comprised two cohort studies, three case series, and three case reports. All were conducted in the United States between 2009 and 2024. Sample sizes ranged from single cases to 1540 participants. Studies were conducted in both hospital and pre-hospital settings, with study durations ranging from 4 days to 4 years. Type-specific WB was provided, when available, to women with a known blood type and negative antibody screen (“typically” limited to O-positive or A-positive). Otherwise, PRBCs would be given. The CT group received a significantly greater number of transfused products (mean 5.5 units, with 72% receiving only WB and PRBCs) than the WB (2.2 units) or PRBC (2.3 units) groups (p <.001). Placental previa or abruption, hysterectomy, and perineal trauma were all increased in the CT group, and it was noted that this group was associated with more serious obstetric hemorrhages. Maternal complications, including acute kidney injury (defined as a serum creatinine of ≥1.6 mg/dL in a woman with normal prior renal function, and termed “acute tubular necrosis” in the paper), pulmonary edema, adult respiratory distress syndrome, hypofibrinogenemia, and ICU admission, were significantly more common in the CT group (Table 2). Maternal deaths occurred in the CT (n = 2) and PRBC-only (n = 1) groups; none were reported in the WB-only group. Munoz et al. conducted a prospective cohort study of 34 patients with placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) who received transfusions at the University of Texas Health San Antonio.21 Sixteen patients received ≤4 units of WB, and 18 received component therapy only. No statistically significant differences were found in operative time, reoperation rates, length of stay, or infection rates. Transfusion volumes were significantly lower in the WB group (2607 mL vs. 4683 mL, p = .03), though volumes were estimated using standard values rather than actual administered volumes. Three case series were identified.20, 25, 24 Morris et al. reported on seven patients from 2 centers: Intermountain Medical Center (IMC) and University of Texas Health San Antonio (UTHSA).20 At IMC, uncrossmatched, RhD-negative low titer type-O whole blood (LTOWB) was used in emergency transfusion of women of child-bearing potential. Four patients (aged 19–38 years) received a total of 10 units of LTOWB (4 units to 1 patient, 2 units each to the other 3). Effective hemorrhage control was reported in all cases, with no deaths or severe adverse transfusion reactions reported. However, 1 patient required additional blood components and uterine artery embolization. At UTHSA, the protocol planned for LTOWB in selected high-risk obstetric patients with high-risk placental abnormalities, confirmed ABO and RhD types, and a negative antibody screen with no history of allo-antibodies. Seven units were administered to 3 patients. All patients were type O+ with only one patient having a positive antibody screen (Anti-M). Effective hemorrhage control was reported in all cases, with no deaths or severe adverse transfusion reactions observed. All patients underwent hysterectomy, two of which were planned. Smith et al. described WB transfusion in 55 non-trauma patients, including 6 obstetric cases.24 Outcomes were not reported separately for obstetric patients. Overall, in-hospital mortality was 30.9%. Transfusion-related adverse events occurred in 5.5% of cases (n = 3), including one mild and two severe allergic reactions. Carr et al. described 25 obstetric patients who received LTOWB as the initial transfusion product for postpartum hemorrhage at Intermountain Medical Center.25 The median estimated blood loss was 3250 mL and the median number of LTOWB units transfused was three (range 1–8). No transfusion-related adverse reactions were reported. Hysterectomy was performed in 16% of patients, and maternal death occurred in 8%. Three case reports were included.19, 22, 23 Bahr et al. a 33-year-old woman with postpartum hemorrhage who received two units of LTOWB followed by plasma and PRBCs.19 She experienced no transfusion-related complications and was discharged on hospital day four. Newberry et al. described a prehospital case in which a 27-year-old patient with placenta previa and suspected accreta received 500 mL of LTOWB en route to hospital.22 She underwent emergency cesarean section and hysterectomy, followed by additional PRBC transfusions during and after surgery, and was discharged in stable condition on postoperative day three without complications. Polzin et al. described two patients who received LTOWB during air transport.23 The first patient received 3 units of O-negative PRBC for hemorrhage related to an ectopic pregnancy at 5–6 weeks gestational age (GA), followed by 1 unit of LTOWB during transport to a tertiary care facility. Anti-D immune globulin was given post-operatively. The second patient received 1 unit of LTOWB for vaginal bleeding following emergency C-section at 39 weeks GA. The LTOWB was given during transport to a tertiary care center. The patient was admitted to the ICU for 1 day after the indicated laparotomy. Both patients recovered without transfusion-related complications and were discharged in stable condition. This scoping review describes the existing literature on the use of WB in the obstetric population. Published evidence is limited with a single-center prospective, observational, cohort study representing the highest quality evidence identified, and multiple publications describing experience from the same academic center. While the findings of this review do not raise any major safety concerns with the use of WB in obstetric hemorrhage, assessment for harm in the existing evidence was not robustly measured. The evidence of clinical benefit is very limited, with WB associated with lower transfusion volume in one study21 and lower risk of AKI in another.18 Long-term follow-up of alloimmunization risk was not reported in any study. The benefits and safety of WB in the management of obstetric hemorrhage is uncertain and requires further study. Two cohort studies provided comparisons of women transfused WB and those transfused conventional components. Both are limited by small sample size and observational design. It is unknown if the women transfused with WB would have had similarly favorable outcomes if they were initially transfused RBCs. Both studies excluded women with positive antibody screens from receiving WB, limiting the generalizability to alloimmunized women. Confounding by degree of illness is possible, particularly in the study from Alexander et al., since the group that received exclusively WB or RBCs had lower American Society of Anesthesiology class. The higher transfusion requirements may reflect bias toward a more unwell population in the combined therapy group. Selection bias is also likely in this study, as WB was only given to women if blood typing was complete (selecting for less urgent cases) and antibody screen is negative (selecting for primigravid patients). Women who received WB and needed additional component therapy were evaluated separately from women who received exclusively WB, introducing survival bias to the WB-only group. Outcomes potentially appear more favorable because more severely bleeding women were transfused additional products and were analyzed as a separate group. The ability to provide a balanced resuscitation with a single blood product is appealing as it simplifies the transfusion process, which is hypothesized to be of benefit in emergency and resource-limited settings such as during the transportation of a patient, but our review identified insufficient evidence to support or refute superiority of WB on clinical outcomes. Although WB may simplify transfusion by delivering red cells, platelets, and plasma in one product, its use in obstetric care presents specific challenges. The risk of RhD alloimmunization is an important consideration, particularly in settings where RhD-negative WB is limited.26 None of the included studies reported long-term alloimmunization outcomes. In the case series by Morris et al., RhD-negative WB was used at one center, while RhD-positive patients were selected at another.20 For patients with Placental Accreta Spectrum, the high likelihood of hysterectomy adds uncertainty to the obstetric relevance of alloimmunization, as mentioned in the UTHSA study.20 While alloimmunization can occur not only against the RhD antigen but also against other blood group antigens (e.g. Kidd, Duffy, etc.), this risk is not increased with WB compared with component therapy strategies, since these antigen systems are not routinely considered in selecting PRBCs for transfusion, in the absence of previously identified antibodies. Therefore, the overall risk of alloimmunization in this context remains unclear. Yazer et al. conducted a simulation study to estimate the trade-off between mortality reduction and RhD alloimmunization in females of childbearing potential.10 The model suggested that any relative mortality reduction greater than 0.1% with WB would offset the theoretical long-term risks. This simulation focused on trauma patients and may not be directly applicable to obstetric populations. In obstetric hemorrhage, the balance between short-term clinical benefit and long-term reproductive risk remains uncertain. Compared to obstetric care, WB transfusion has been more extensively studied in trauma populations. Several studies have reported associations between WB use and reductions in early mortality and transfusion requirements in trauma patients.27-30 Recent meta-analyses have reported that WB resuscitation may be associated with improved early survival among patients with hemorrhagic trauma.7, 31 These findings have informed the implementation of WB protocols in various settings. However, extension to obstetric hemorrhage is limited by differences in the clinical context. Trauma studies often involve young male patients with hemorrhage secondary to blunt or penetrating injury. In contrast, obstetric hemorrhage results from different etiologies, such as uterine atony or placental disorders, and occurs in pregnant individuals with distinct physiological considerations.32 Coagulopathy profiles and transfusion priorities also differ between these populations. Moreover, trauma studies typically do not include subgroup analyses focused on pregnant patients, which limits their applicability. While the trauma literature contributes important information regarding WB logistics and feasibility, its relevance to obstetric care remains uncertain without studies specifically addressing this population. For blood operators, the logistic advantages of WB transfusion must be weighed against the impact WB manufacturing could have on the blood supply. The production of a unit of WB comes at the “cost” of a unit of PRBCs, a unit of plasma, and part of a unit of pooled platelets. Depending on the storage medium used, the shelf-life range of WB is lower than PRBCs (21–35 days vs. 35–42 days), adding additional pressure on PRBC supply.33-35 Some blood centers have implemented salvage protocols, whereby PRBCs are derived from expiring WB units.36 Preclinical studies support the functional equivalence of salvaged PRBCs with standard products.36 Salvaged PRBC could represent a viable option for the recycling of expiring and stored WB, a practice already used in many American centers. The implications on the blood supply are justifiable if clinical outcomes are improved by WB transfusion. However, this review identified a lack of evidence to support WB as a superior resuscitation strategy compared with component therapy for obstetric hemorrhage. The evidence for WB as a superior transfusion strategy in trauma is not convincing.31 Until WB is demonstrated to offer an advantage in relevant clinical outcomes, the trade-off in shorter shelf-life may not be worth the challenges it could cause on the blood supply. This study followed established scoping review methodology, including a peer-reviewed search strategy and involvement of a multidisciplinary team. Despite these strengths, several limitations warrant consideration. The review included only studies published in English or French, which may have excluded relevant data from non-English or French sources. All included studies were conducted in the United States, which may limit the applicability of findings to other health systems with different transfusion protocols, infrastructure, or resource availability. No randomized controlled trials were identified, and critical appraisal of study quality was not conducted, consistent with scoping review methodology. Several studies excluded patients with positive antibody screens, limiting generalizability to alloimmunized populations. Additionally, case reports and case series often described highly selected clinical scenarios, which may not reflect routine obstetric practice.
